text: Jürgen Walther Ludwig Aschoff (January 25, 1913 – October 12, 1998) was a German physician, biologist, and behavioral physiologist recognized as a co-founder of chronobiology alongside Erwin Bünning and Colin Pittendrigh. His research introduced Aschoff's Rules, which describe light interactions in the circadian rhythms of nocturnal and diurnal species. Born in Freiburg im Breisgau as the fifth child of pathologist Ludwig Aschoff and Clara, he grew up in the liberal yet morally strict environment of Prussian academia. After completing his Abitur at a humanistic high school, he studied medicine at the University of Bonn, where he joined the Burschenschaft Alemannia Bonn. His scientific career began in 1938 when he moved to the University of Göttingen to study thermoregulation physiology under Hermann Rein, earning the venia legendi in 1944 and becoming a professor there in 1949. In 1952, Rein transferred to the Max Planck Institute for Medical Research in Heidelberg, bringing Aschoff to collaborate on circadian rhythms in humans, birds, and mice. Aschoff then moved to the Max Planck Institute for Behavioral Physiology in Andechs to work with Gustav Kramer and Erich von Holst. From 1967 to 1979, he served as director at the Max Planck Institute for Behavioral Physiology and as a professor in Munich. He was a scientific member and member of the Kollegiums at the institute and served as senator of the Max Planck Society from 1972 to 1976. Known for his excellent lecturing and dedication to fostering scientific communities, Aschoff continued publishing after retiring in 1983 and returning to Freiburg, dying in 1998 at age 85, just ten months after his wife Hilde’s death. His early work focused on thermoregulation, where he discovered a 24-hour rhythm in body temperature, leading to investigations into circadian mechanisms. In the 1950s, he collaborated with Bünning and Pittendrigh, conducting experiments on birds and mice under constant conditions, concluding that circadian oscillations are innate and do not require prior exposure to a 24-hour day. In 1960, he coined the term "Zeitgeber" (time giver or synchronizer) to describe external cues that align endogenous oscillators with environmental cycles. Experiments in constant light revealed that nocturnal organisms exhibit shortened activity phases (alpha compression) and diurnal organisms show lengthened phases (alpha expansion), later formalized as Aschoff's Rule. This rule, which states that the free-running period (τ) of nocturnal organisms in constant darkness (DD) is less than 24 hours (τDD < 24), and in constant light (LL) is greater than 24 hours (τLL > 24), is further expanded to Tau = f(LL-intensity). Rule 3 states that increasing light intensity in LL lengthens the free-running period in nocturnal organisms, while Rule 4 states that the same increase shortens the period in diurnal organisms. Exceptions exist, such as in ground beetles and squirrels, which do not follow Rule 1, and some arthropods that may violate Rule 3 due to prior lighting history. Aschoff's human studies involved isolating subjects in an underground bunker with no external cues, where participants reported their sleep-wake cycles, body temperature, and urine output. Over twenty years, Aschoff and Rütger Wever found that humans possess endogenous circadian oscillators, with free-running periods ranging from 23.56 to 24.7 hours, and that social cues like meal times can serve as Zeitgebers for entrainment. In constant darkness, some subjects showed desynchronization between body temperature and sleep-wake cycles, with rectal temperature at sleep onset correlating to sleep duration, leading Aschoff to hypothesize that internal desynchronization may relate to psychiatric disorders. He also identified a circadian rhythm in thermal conductance, allowing animals to release heat during activity and conserve it during rest, with birds relying on evaporative heat loss and mammals on changes in heat resistance and blood flow. He found that temperature can entrain mammals but is a weaker Zeitgeber than light. Aschoff described masking signals as inputs that affect circadian behavior without acting on the pacemaker, and proposed "arousal" as a response to non-photic Zeitgebers. He concluded that the circadian clock integrates light intensity over time and adjusts its period accordingly, with parametric entrainment being a key mechanism. His work inspired research into blue light, molecular mechanisms of circadian rhythms, and the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN). At the Chinese Academy of Sciences, the Wang lab studied blue light's effect on CRY2 and PRR9 interactions in plants, showing that blue light stimulates CRY2 to block PRR9 from interacting with co-repressors and kinases, altering PRR9 phosphorylation and thus circadian timing. In the Foster lab at Imperial College, London, researchers found that in constant darkness, mPer1, mPer2, mCry1, and mCry2 showed rhythmic expression, while in constant light, mCry2 rhythms were altered, and mice had longer free-running periods (24.47 hours vs. 23.26 hours), suggesting mPER2 contributes to phase delays. In the Yoon lab at the University of Aveiro, Portugal, researchers found that the core-shell organization of the SCN, with the shell (ventral) peaking before the core, enables anticipation of external stimuli and supports Aschoff's first rule. At a 1991 Gordon Conference dinner honoring Aschoff, Professor Till Roenneberg established the "Aschoff's Rule Prize" to recognize contributions to chronobiology, first awarded to Professor Maroli K. Chandrashekera in 1991, with recipients selecting the next winner annually under two guidelines. Aschoff also published with Serge Daan, a key figure in chronobiology, and Daan's 2008 research provided evidence supporting Aschoff's parametric model of entrainment, despite the field now recognizing multiple models. Daan died in 2018.
